content.overview: Section 2 is the interpretation-clause. Unless a contrary intention appears from the context: (a) a proposal is a signification of willingness to do or abstain from doing something with a view to obtaining the other’s assent; (b) acceptance turns a proposal into a promise; (c) the maker is the promisor and the acceptor the promisee; (d) consideration is an act, abstinence or promise at the desire of the promisor by the promisee or any other person; (e) every promise and every set of promises forming consideration for each other is an agreement; (f) reciprocal promises form consideration for each other; (g) an agreement not enforceable by law is void; (h) an agreement enforceable by law is a contract; (i) an agreement enforceable at the option of one or more parties but not the other is a voidable contract; (j) a contract which ceases to be enforceable by law becomes void when it ceases to be enforceable.
content.glance: Core definitions: proposal → acceptance → promise → agreement → contract; consideration; void / voidable / becomes void.
content.study: Section 2 supplies the vocabulary of the Act. A proposal is willingness to do or abstain with a view to assent. Acceptance makes a promise. Consideration is an act, abstinence or promise at the promisor’s desire by the promisee or any other person. Mutual promises forming consideration are an agreement; enforceable agreements are contracts. Void means not enforceable by law; voidable means enforceable at one party’s option; a contract becomes void when it ceases to be enforceable. Current-law framing: map the facts to the defined terms before applying later sections (e.g. ss. 10, 23–25).

sections.heading: Proposal, acceptance, promise
sections.body: (a)–(c): proposal; acceptance turns proposal into promise; promisor and promisee.

sections.heading: Consideration and agreement
sections.body: (d)–(f): consideration (including by any other person); agreement; reciprocal promises.

sections.heading: Void, contract, voidable, becomes void
sections.body: (g)–(j): void agreement; contract; voidable contract; contract that becomes void.

examples.title: Proposal and acceptance
examples.body: A signifies willingness to sell goods to B with a view to B’s assent. B signifies assent. The proposal becomes a promise under s. 2(b).

hypotheticals.question: Is every agreement a contract?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Under s. 2(g)–(h), only an agreement enforceable by law is a contract; an agreement not enforceable by law is void.

distinctions.title: Void agreement (s. 2(g)) vs voidable contract (s. 2(i))
distinctions.right: Enforceable at the option of one or more parties but not the other

misconceptions.trap: Void and voidable mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Void (s. 2(g)) is not enforceable by law; voidable (s. 2(i)) is enforceable at one party’s option.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 2 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the defined term in issue. II. Apply the statutory sense unless context shows contrary intention. III. Map to later operative sections. IV. Conclude.

examTips: Know the chain: proposal → promise → agreement → contract.
Distinguish void, voidable, and becomes void.
